extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and journalism students (news writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing news stories about politics (especially elections) and labor troubles/strikes, covering types of election pieces, what to include in returns and election-day coverage, and how to handle strike reporting. Aimed at practical newsroom coverage decisions and story elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three common kinds of election stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Three common kinds of election stories are: (1) an analysis of political conditions preceding an election with or without a forecast of the result, (2) a description of election day conditions and events, (3) the results of the election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elections require a different handling than ordinary political items; choose the type of story (forecast/analysis, election-day description, or returns) and structure content accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political reporting impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Although some newspapers are sufficiently independent in politics to treat political news without partisan bias, many papers still present such news from the point of view of their editorial policy. There is a growing tendency, however, to present both sides fairly in news columns and to confine partisanship to editorials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present both sides fairly in news columns; reserve explicit partisanship for editorials. Strive for balanced coverage even if the paper has an editorial stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election return stories — essential content elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Election return stories consist largely of summaries of the most important results of the election, such as: (1) the candidates elected and defeated, (2) the majority or plurality of the successful candidates, (3) the effect of the election on the political complexion of legislative bodies, (4) causes of victory and defeat, (5) statements by candidates and party managers in regard to the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure returns include who won/lost, margins (majorities/pluralities), implications for legislative control, analysis of causes, and quoted reactions from key actors. Use these five elements as a checklist for returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political forecast/analysis should use local evidence and comparative figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Forecasts and analyses should be grounded in local canvassing, historical vote comparisons, and reasoned estimates (e.g., comparing party vote percentages, checking lists, and likely defections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support predictions with concrete figures and local intelligence (check lists, canvasses, past vote behavior). Explain the assumptions (e.g., defections, polling shifts) and show the arithmetic or logic leading to the forecast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election-day reporting — report turnout timing and patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe voting patterns (early rush, lulls, percent of vote by certain hours), record-breaking early voting, and how turnout progressed during the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use time-stamped turnout figures (e.g., percent by noon, percent by 4 p.m.) and anecdotal markers to convey the pace and character of the day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election-day reporting — ballot and voting-process problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Report problems or ease with ballots and voting procedures (e.g., trouble expected from new ballots; use of sample ballots and instructors to reduce confusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note whether new or modified ballots caused delays or confusion; describe measures taken (sample voting places, instructors) and typical time-per-voter to indicate whether the process functioned smoothly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election-day reporting — report irregularities, challenges, and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Record challenges to voters, arrests or attempts to enforce voting law (e.g., 'place of stay' watchers, squads searching for fraud), disputes over election inspectors, and deployment of special inspectors when legal requirements aren't met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document incidents (who objected, basis of objection), legal provisions violated (e.g., number of inspectors required), official responses (sending special inspectors, deputies), and final disposition to show how issues affected voting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election-day reporting — human-interest and notable-person details
rubrics_metrics.description: Include human-interest details and notable presences (volunteer watcher squads, former sports stars acting as watchers, humorous anecdotes like deserted polling places).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognizable personalities, vivid anecdotes, and small human details to enliven election-day copy while keeping the focus on the electoral process; such items can illustrate civic engagement or the day's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor/strike reporting — present both sides and include statements from employers and employees
rubrics_metrics.description: A fair and accurate presentation of the points of view of both the employers and the employees is essential in all stories of this kind. Statements from both sides, therefore, are important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit and quote official statements from management and union leaders as well as rank-and-file workers; avoid one-sided portrayals and make clear contrasting positions and demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor/strike reporting — include human-interest accounts of living and working conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Although stories in this class are largely informative, there is also a chance for human interest treatment. Accounts of living and working conditions, for example, as obtained from workmen and their families often give a better picture of the circumstances that produced the strike than do formal statements by labor leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interview workers and families about day-to-day conditions to provide context and explain the causes of unrest; use such material to humanize the story while corroborating with facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor/strike reporting — legitimate sympathy but factual completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Sympathy may be legitimately created for the strikers and their families, especially when they are in actual want or are plainly the victims of oppression. Because the settlement of labor troubles not infrequently is brought about by the influence of public opinion, constructive journalism recognizes the importance of furnishing readers with all of the facts necessary for an intelligent understanding of the issues and conditions involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to evoke sympathy when supported by facts, but always provide the full factual background so readers can make an informed judgment; present evidence for claims of hardship or oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor/strike reporting — report demands, bargaining positions, and arbitration options
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe what the union demands (wages, hours, seniority, representation after promotion), the employers' counteroffers (e.g., half-holidays, overtime pay), and whether arbitration (such as under statutes like the Erdman Act) is proposed or rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail the specific issues in dispute, any proposals to arbitrate, the union's and employers' willingness to submit to third-party resolution, and why one side accepts or rejects arbitration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor/strike reporting — report scale, scope, and potential economic impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Report numbers involved (employees, trains, railroads, miles of track affected), how many systems or employers could be tied up, and secondary effects (other workers likely to be thrown out, sympathetic strikes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify the strike's reach and likely consequences; use figures (number of workers, companies affected, geographic scope) to convey seriousness and potential disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strike incident reporting — report violence, casualties, and tactical details
rubrics_metrics.description: When clashes occur, report casualties, missing persons, wounded, alleged actions (e.g., setting fire to tents), forces involved (militia, state troops, strikers), armaments and ammunition, tactical movements, and appeals for external aid (consuls, Red Cross).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide precise numbers, identify parties and units involved, describe sequence of events, and note humanitarian or international dimensions; corroborate violent-incident claims carefully due to their gravity.
